And I'm referring to the year 1992. What was his position or what was the SDS position to other nations living in the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: After the elections, the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the war broke out, does it mean that there were no longer any speeches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: There were speeches but we were not able to listen to them regularly because we had no electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how would you describe the reason why people were leaving? Was it just because -- because of the -- cause in Banja Luka or what else made them to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: I think they were leaving for the same reasons that the Serbs were arriving in Banja Luka. People feared retaliation. As the Serbs came to Banja Luka, at the same time, the non-Serbs left for other places. They were afraid to stay, but I can't say that any of the politicians made the people move. On any side. I know what people said in the agency. Every non-Serb who was on good terms with me and whom I asked why he was leaving, each and every one of them said I am leaving because I am afraid some of the Serbs who have arrived who have been driven out of their towns will drive me out or kill me. And I want to protect my children and so on. I never heard anyone while working at the agency and I really want to tell you the real truth now, I never heard anyone say that someone in authority was forcing them to leave. At least the people who had contacts with me and who have now returned to Banja Luka and we are in contact again now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall answering to the question, again it was the very similar questions whether any of these comments could make people to leave the city, it's page 38, and you said, "Definitely, surely not positive since they decided to leave the city." And when Mr. Dupas asked you, do you think that some of the things he said, and the discussion was about Mr. Brdjanin, he said inspired people to leave? And your answer was -- was "Yes." So this wasn't true, what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No, no. That's not how I understood it. I said today that I was very confused when I had my first interview. Not for a moment did I understand that I was to testify here either for or against Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not testifying for or against anyone here. You're testifying towards the truth. We are in -- we have a common enterprise here. We are searching for the truth. So please do not look at your testimony as being a testimony for or against someone. You have a responsibility here to tell us the truth. And the question that was asked of you by Mr. Dupas in the interview couldn't have confused your mind, because it was a very simple and clear question. He was referring to the interventions of Mr. Brdjanin that you had spoken about earlier on in the course of the interview, and he told you, Mr. Dupas, well, let's talk about some of the things he did, he did speak about. What do you think was the impact of the things that he was saying on the Serb -- on the non-Serb population? And you said, "Definitely, surely not positive, since they decided to leave the city." And Mr. Dupas told you, do you think that some of the things that he said -- do you think that some of the things that he said inspired people to leave? And you said, "Yes." And then what's most important of all, Mr. Dupas told you, did people actually tell you that? And you said, "No." So you made up this conclusion yourself. You reached this conclusion yourself. Not other people telling you that they had been inspired by Mr. Brdjanin to leave. This is the conclusion that you arrived at. Why did you arrive at that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. That's not the way I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. I think that's enough from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And actually, Judge Janu is drawing my attention to another part of your testimony soon after that you had just confirmed to Mr. Dupas that this was your own conclusion that you had arrived at. And then you said, "My personal stance was such that when I looked at him, and while listening to his speeches and the way he, when he, when he was, his appearance, and I was thinking what an idiot you are, I mean I've been living with these people for 50 years or 30 years, I don't know, and you're trying to, you know, to create a conflict between us, you know, so that that was my personal stance, the members of the HDZ and the -- or the SDA were no better. They all said the same thing. I experienced this for me, this was a very, very difficult experience because it was a psychological burden on me." So please, do tell us the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am telling the truth. And I was referring to all three sides, because there was an ethnic war going on there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were referring to all three parties, but just non-Serb population was leaving from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: But the Serb population was coming to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But non-Serb population was leaving Banja Luka because they were afraid of their lives? And we are talking about political parties in Banja Luka. So it wasn't Serb who would leave the Banja Luka because they would be afraid.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: The Serbs were not leaving Banja Luka. They were arriving in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I don't have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Madam Richterova. Mr. Ackerman? Mr. Ackerman will be putting some questions to you, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, madam, how are you this morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Pretty good, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused, ma'am, because when you spoke with the Prosecutor in Banja Luka, about this agency, you indicated at that time that you did not believe that the agency got involved with assisting non-Serb persons to leave Banja Luka until October of 1992. I think what you said, it didn't begin doing that kind of work until it had become officially registered, which actually happened in October. Is that your recollection or were you confused at that time? Did it start a bit earlier? What's the best you can tell us regarding that now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No. In my work booklet, the copy of which I provided to the Office of the Prosecutor, it says, in accordance with our law, the work experience is mentioned there, in order not to have any interruptions, any breaks in service, when my company ceased working, I paid adequate contributions into the fund and I wanted to link my work experience in the company with my work in the agency, and hence the stamp, which was a bit confusing perhaps in the beginning. I must say that I was confused when I was summoned to the interview and I needed sometime to refresh my memory. So when I stopped working in December, I started paying appropriate contribution in the pension fund so that I could have entire pension when

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think must --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman, we need to redact the -- in line 22, and in line 24, the two names that appear there. I need not mention them here because then I would have to redact what I am saying too. Page 58, lines 22 and 24. Yes, go ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The part I was actually confused about, ma'am, was when the agency began assisting non-Serbs who were wanting to leave the Banja Luka area and you had said during this interview in Banja Luka that you believed that was October of 1992 but then today you told us that it could have been as early as August of 1992, and I'm just wondering, giving this your best recollection, which of those you think it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: I think it was August. I was a bit confused by the stamp for October in that work booklet and that's why I mentioned October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. Now, you told us about the fares that people were paying, they were paying somewhere between 30 and 50 deutschmarks for their bus fares, you told us, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact price.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. I would like the Registrar to give you three documents. They are the three Y001 documents, 8259, 8261, 8263. I'd like you to have all those available to look at for a moment. The first one I'd like you to look at, ma'am, is a document I think it's 8262, 8263, it's a payroll for July of 1992. Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that document contains your name and shows that you were paid a net amount of 20.000 dinars, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- first thing I want to ask you is: Can you give us any kind of an approximation as to about how many deutschmarks 20.000 dinars would have been in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: I really cannot recall what the rate was, but I think it was less than 100 deutschmarks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at the bottom of that document, because one of the concerns is why is this July of 1992, when the company didn't start until later, if you look at the bottom, you'll notice, don't you, that the document is actually dated 30 September, 1992. You see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that the date, July, 1992, was a mistake on this document? And that it actually should have been an August or September date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: It could have been a mistake, but it's also possible that at the time we did not have enough money so we didn't pay the salaries until September when they were paid retroactively. These are the two possibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if the Prosecution intends to make this document an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. I forgot to tender all these three documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you will both do that at the end of the witness's testimony, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's going to be very confusing for someone trying to find out in the transcript what it is we are talking about, because for instance the document I have doesn't have any of these Y numbers that the Prosecution has put on them. And I don't know if the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Ackerman is right here. Perhaps you can tell us straight away, Madam Richterova, this last document that we are talking about, the payroll for July, with Y001-8263, and then BD0657E, what exhibit number you intend giving it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It would be P1687. And it would be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So be it. And the other one, the December?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The payroll for December, Y001-8259, would be 1688.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Under seal. And the Y001-8261 would be 1689.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, while we are looking at those documents, the other one that you've not looked at yet is now called P1689, you'll find I think on that document the number BD0656. And that is a document called an authorisation. It has to do with authorising certain persons to travel to Croatia, and although that document contains a heading, "Autonomous Region of Krajina, Banja Luka" it's actually signed, is it not, by Milos Bojinovic, the director of the agency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. These fares that people were paying, this 30 to 50 deutschmark fares that people were paying for their bus fares, would you say these were normal bus fares for -- that people would be required to pay for the kind of transportation they were receiving or were they kind of outrageously high numbers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Not outrageously high numbers. It is true that we paid a lot of money for the transport. The oil was four German marks at the time so I don't think that the price was too high. But I wasn't the one who established the price, and I don't remember exactly what it was, between 30 and 50 German marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked to a lot of these people. Did any of them complain that the bus fares were way too high or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these people, to the extent that you spoke with them and understood what they were doing, these were people who were wanting to leave Banja Luka, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were trying very hard to get their names on the lists of those that were permitted to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you have told us that there were several reasons that they wanted to leave, primary among them was their fear of retaliation from the Serbs who were coming in to the city from other places, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these Serbs who were coming into the city from other places, from other parts of Bosnia and from Croatia, were people that -- that had been basically thrown out of their homes and made to become refugees and came to Banja Luka as a safe place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: That's what they told us when they came to the agency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they came there with an attitude, they came there angry, for what had happened to them, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the fear of the non-Serb population of Banja Luka regarding the possibility of retaliation, was not an unwarranted fear, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other reasons that people were wanting to leave was Banja Luka was a place that had very little food and that had no electricity much of the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This whole business of people going to the SUP to cancel their residence, that was the law of former Yugoslavia, wasn't it? If you were going to move from one place to another, you had to go to the SUP and tell them you were moving, cancel your residence in the place, in that place, so you could take up residence in a new place? You had to do that, everybody, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that went on way before there was any multiple parties or war or anything of this -- these things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Before the war as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the non-Serb people who travelled through the assistance of your agency ever required to sign over any of their property to the government before they could leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've told us that all the people who wanted to leave, a condition of their being able to leave, was that if they were going to a third country, if they were going to some place like Germany or Spain or France, that they had to have a letter of guarantee from these places saying that they would be permitted to enter these countries once they arrived there, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes. It applied also to those who wanted to go to Croatia. They also had to have a letter of guarantee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when you went to -- when you went to the border with Croatia to exchange documents, these guarantees, wasn't that a two-way exchange? Didn't you also furnish guarantees to the Croatian government regarding Serbian people who were coming to Banja Luka? Or was it just a one-way thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No, no. We only received letters of guarantee for non-Serb population who wanted to leave Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when these people would be accepted, put on the list, and come and get on the bus, from your observations, nobody took from them any jewellery or any valuables or anything like that? Nobody stole these things from their luggage, to your knowledge, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No, no. No convoy left without passengers having been escorted by the members of their families who for whatever reasons were still there, were not leaving yet because they had not sold all their furniture or were still waiting for the letter of guarantee or were not able to collect all the necessary documents. They were there to say goodbye to their mothers and friends, and it was all happening there and we could see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just to get a sort of mental picture of the scene, it begins with a list being posted on your office of the people who had been authorised for the next transport? Then there is a date and a time, the buses are there, the people come with all of their belongings that they want to bring with them, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with them are relatives and friends there to see them off, and kiss them goodbye and things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: A day or two before that, we were required to put those lists on a board so that the people could find their names, together with the date of departure. The buses would usually depart early in the morning, around 7.00 or 8.00 and the people would come to the agency with their luggage, board the buses, say goodbye to their friends and relatives and leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're there, you're observing what's going on at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... these other non-Serb people are there observing what's going on there at the time, who are not going on the transport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the only searches that took place that you observed or that you knew about were searches for prohibited items like weapons, cameras, military identifications, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you told the Prosecutor during your interview in Banja Luka, you can say with full responsibility that everything was done correctly, can't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin never appeared at your agency, did he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't personally know him, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you had heard of him? Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw him on television in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But today, you can't remember any specific thing that you heard him say on television, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, as you told the Prosecutor during your interview in Banja Luka, that you also heard SDA leaders on television at the same time urging Muslims to arm themselves against the Serbs. Do you remember hearing speeches like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you know, these speeches that you heard, made by Mr. Brdjanin or by these SDA leaders or even maybe some HDZ people, these speeches all occurred in 1991, early 1992, before there was ever any Crisis Staff in existence in Banja Luka, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She said "da."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You answered yes to that last question, didn't you, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This might be a good time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to suggest to you to look at the clock. How much longer do you think -- do you envisage you will take, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It looks to me like 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 20 minutes. Okay. So -- no, because we definitely have to stop at half past 1.00 because there is a 65 ter meeting in another case that I have to be present at. You have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, but, Your Honour, the witness asked me that she definitely needs to leave The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm trying to make sure that she will be able to leave, in fact. Can we shorten the break to 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm quite certain I won't be more than 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if there is re-examination plus some questions from the bench, is it okay with you, 15 minutes? All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we need more time, we can go on without a break, I'm doing fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It's for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 15 minutes' break, 15 minutes' break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, could you tell us who you remember as being the political leaders in Banja Luka during 1992? What names do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: All three ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or what was left of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The political leaders that you can remember, what were their names?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1992, we want to know, not 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brdjanin, Mr. Kupresanin, Mr. Radic, Mr. Lutovic. He was the President of the SDA, I think. I can't remember many of them. There was Mr. Krzic, I think that's what his Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. name was. But I can't recall any other names now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Kupresanin. Do you have any recollection of what position he held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Mr. Radic was the mayor of the municipality, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had mentioned during your direct examination that during the time when the Red Cross was handling these transfers of people who were leaving Banja Luka, that you had many school friends and colleagues who left during that time, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these were people who you talked to, people who you said goodbye to, people who you knew at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were these people leaving voluntarily? Were they people who were leaving because they wanted to leave or did they tell you they were being forced to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No. No one told me that they had been forced to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you ever recall at any time hearing Mr. Brdjanin make any speeches against war profiteers and against paramilitary organisations, or either one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Would you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall at any time hearing Mr. Brdjanin make any speeches where he was being critical, war he was against war profiteers or paramilitary organisations? Do you recall him saying anything like that in any of his speeches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: I almost never heard any speech of Mr. Brdjanin's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer is you never heard him saying anything like what I just suggested? And I take it that you also never heard him saying that everything had to be done according to the law?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from any of your non-Serb friends, either at the time or since they have returned to Banja Luka, that Mr. Brdjanin had actually helped them in some way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No. I really have to tell you quite truthfully, none of them ever mentioned Mr. Brdjanin to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to private session for just a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think during your interview with the Prosecutor, you were talking about how people were afraid of retaliation and this needs to be in private session again, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go to private session, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, we are in open session, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said with regard to that period in 1995, that it was a time when many, many non-Serbs left the town. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The way you explained it was because -- let me give your full answer. "People were afraid of retaliation, just like Serbs were afraid of retaliation in Sarajevo, so were the Muslims afraid of retaliation here. I will now tell you a story of a friend of mine who was a good acquaintance of mine," and I won't say her name and I'll skip over that part, "she left Banja Luka in 1995, when Krajina fell. When all those people came to Banja Luka, this was the time when many, many non-Serbs left town." And when you say when all those people came to Banja Luka, you're referring, are you not, to a large number of Serb refugees who arrived in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went on to say, "Because when those people came, they naturally kicked the Muslims out, they chased them out from here without anyone's asking them to do so. And she told me, I want to leave here for one and only reason because I don't want a Serb who had been expelled from Glamoc or God knows where else from to come here to my door and to kick me out of my apartment because he was kicked out of his over there, and I don't want to start hating my Serbian friends because of it." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, you described conditions in Banja Luka as being horrible for all nationalities. You said there were periods of 45 days without electricity, and that there was a curfew that applied to everyone, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if someone were to describe Banja Luka in 1992 as a ghetto for non-Serbs, I take it you would not agree with that but that it was difficult for everyone just the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your interview with the Prosecutor, you said that there were no barricades set up in Banja Luka in April, 1992, by anyone, including an organisation they referred to called SOS. And that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: That's correct. There were no barricades in the town. Could the interpreter speak up? I don't hear very well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher, could you please move the microphones nearer to the speaker, to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's that she is not hearing, not that they are not hearing her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, she's not hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She's not hearing well, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's correct, I don't hear very well, could it just be a little louder please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then could you adjust the volume on her -- is it better now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said during that interview that one of the reasons you knew that there were no barricades in April of 1992 or during that time was that you yourself were able to move around freely and to have coffee with your non-Serb friends, that you went to visit them and they came to visit you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: We could all move about, regardless of our ethnicity because there were really no barricades in the town itself. There were checkpoints at the exit and entry points but within the town, everybody moved around freely, both Serbs and non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we go to private session again, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go to private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the transports, the buses that were taking non-Serb people out of Banja Luka, to your knowledge, the army was not involved in any of these convoys, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No, only the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the agency, there were, in addition to the non-Serb people who were showing up trying to get permission to leave, and get on the lists, at the same time there were Serb refugees who were showing up at the agency also, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that there were even some confrontations that went on at your agency between the Serbs who had been kicked out of the places where they lived, and those non-Serbs who were trying to leave Banja Luka, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: To a lesser extent. Because we had the police who were in charge of law and order, so fights rarely broke out. There were only verbal abuses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the police were there trying to reduce the tensions between these people? To prevent any outbreaks of serious matters? In other words, they were trying to reduce and calm tensions, not to create tensions, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: The police was there so that any conflict could -- would be avoided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to look, please, at the document P238. I believe that's the number. Yeah. Ma'am, at the bottom of that document, there is some handwriting. I'm wondering if you can read that, if you can read what it says in that handwriting there. Because the translation we have has left out some of that. Maybe you can read it better than our translators could. Do you see what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No. I don't think I can read this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the first line, according to the translation I have, says the conclusion under 2 is binding on the secretary for OU. Would you have any idea what OU stands for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your copy good enough so that you can see that it is signed za and then there is a signature there, that it does not have the signature of Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: I don't know what the signature of Mr. Brdjanin looks like, but I do see the word "za".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In your interview with the Prosecutor, on page 45 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, where is the za that you are specifically referring to on this handwritten part of the document? Is it the za at the left of the initials OU or is it some other za, elsewhere, that you're seeing elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you look at that first line, and count three words in from the right, you'll see OU, you'll see za, and then you'll see another word. Right underneath that word, you can see a za.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's very faint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 45 of your interview with the Prosecutor, you were asked the following question by Ms. Korner: "What do you feel about the work that you did for that agency?" And your answer was this: "I think I helped a great many people. Many of them called me and they likened" - I think it should be likened - "and they likened me to Mother Teresa." It's true, isn't it, that a number of people were very grateful to you for your help in helping them leave that situation they found themselves in in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And even today, many of the non-Serb people who you helped leave Banja Luka are grateful to you, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of them have returned and you've talked to them since their return, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just so this whole issue is very clear, this -- this situation that caused the creation of this agency all started with Serb refugees coming to Banja Luka who had been forcibly expelled from their homes in Croatia and elsewhere in Bosnia, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was only then, when these Serb refugees started coming there in large numbers and becoming a retaliation threat to the non-Serb population in Banja Luka, that that non-Serb population started wanting to leave there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they did so willingly and voluntarily because they wanted to leave a place where they were afraid, where they did not have work, where food was scarce, and where there was often no electricity, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: What people do you have in mind? What population are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the non-Serb people. They decided to leave Banja Luka, a place where they were afraid --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did not have work, where food was scarce and where there was no electricity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you helped them to do that, and for that they were and are grateful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, the fears they had about this retaliation, about Serbs coming there angry and starting to kick people out of their homes actually started happening in 1995 when the Krajina fell, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes. Both in 1992 and 1995, in these two years, many people, Serbs, came to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, that's all I have. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Just very short re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Re-examined by Ms. Richterova:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned this non-Serb who remained as director of one company because he responds -- responded to the mobilisation. Do you remember this question and your answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session a bit, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, repeat your question, please, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was your answer to Mr. Ackerman's question and you said they wanted, non-Serbs, to leave because there was not enough food, there was no electricity. Was there no food and no electricity just for non-Serbs or for all Banja Luka population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: The entire population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also stated that no one told you that they were forced to leave, that they were leaving voluntarily, they were leaving voluntarily because they were afraid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All these people were your -- I'm sorry, not all -- but you stated that many of them were your friends and they were leaving the place where they lived for many, many years. Did you hear from them any specific reason why they were leaving, what made them to leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I think this is beyond appropriate redirect. She asked the same question in her direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ackerman is correct, and his objection is being sustained. You did actually ask the question during your examination-in-chief, and he asked the same question. So -- and we have had a reply and answer from the witness. So move to the --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I do not have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Janu do you have any questions? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Madam, can you clarify for the Chamber why did you leave the agency for movement of the population? What were your reasons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: I've already said that. I lost five members of my family, and I was psychologically unstable. I went through a terrible crisis, and of course, many of my friends had left Banja Luka, many of my relatives had arrived in Banja Luka, but they had not been accommodated anywhere and all this was a cause of great stress, so I left the agency for health reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So from December, you didn't work at all? You were just at home and you were not feeling well? Is that the truth? Or you changed for another job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No. I didn't take another job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And your husband, your husband left the agency as well with you or he stayed and worked there, carry on working there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: My husband left before I did because he had been mobilised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Can you please describe your working day in the -- in the agency, especially what you were doing when being there, your husband, what was your husband doing, and the president of the agency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: My working day was like this: I would arrive there, receive the people who came, make lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: 9.00 or 8.00 or we are only talking about the working days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: 8.00, we started at 8.00, we started at 8.00, from 8.00 to 3.00. We received people coming in, of both ethnic groups, and two girls and I drew up lists. One day we would make a list or I would make a list of non-Serbs. The next day of Serbs. Depending on what was given to me on a particular morning to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And the president was every morning assigning people to certain work or was it day by day the same routine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes he assigned specific tasks to us. If there was a crowd at one desk, he would ask one of us to go and help out there. If there were fewer people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So how many desks there were operating simultaneously, receiving people, checking on the papers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: There were three girls receiving people, two working. There was legal advice, where there was a girl receiving people, and then taking them to the lawyer for consultations. There was another person who took care of the financial side. My husband was a driver because our car was put at the disposal of that agency, and he went with Mr. -- what's his name, to take those lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And the president was at the same office with you organising through the day, the daily routine work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes, he had his own office. He would come and see what we were doing, check on our work, contact people, just as we did. He talked to people also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And you said three girls were gathering, compiling those papers. You were one of those girls or you were most senior officially in the office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was one of them. I didn't have any powers greater than the others. We all did everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Did you sometimes accompany the convoy with the people as an administrative body or you never accompanied a convoy to the border? I mean non-Muslim people, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Not as a representative of some sort of administrative body. I did go a few times but that was only if a friend of mine was in the convoy and I wanted to see them off at the border, so I did accompany convoys to the border occasionally but not in an official capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So how many times, can you estimate? I know you don't remember exactly, but how many times did you go with the convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Maybe three or four times, three, I think. I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: That's okay. And in these three cases, nobody was looted during the way or the convoy didn't stop for these purposes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No. The convoy was never stopped. I don't know if other convoys were stopped but the bus that I was on, I'm sure, wasn't stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: That's what I want from you, just witness what you really saw or heard. Do you recall when the Crisis Staff was established? I don't want to know exact date but approximately, which year, and it was the beginning or the middle of the year or -- you cannot help us on this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No, no, I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: You said that many people returned in Banja Luka. Can you give us some names, especially of those who came back to you and thanked you for what you have done for them during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Quite a few people have come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: In percentages, I think 70, I'm sure. I think 70 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: 70 per cent of the number of people who left before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Of the number of people whom I know, who are friends of mine. I want to say not everybody has come back but most of them have. Those who have gone to America -- but I'm talking about non-Serbs whom I consider my friends, those who went to America have not come back but those who went to European have almost all come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And what is the number we are talking, we are discussing, your friends? You said 70 per cent, so there you must have some number on your mind.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: I don't know. A lot of non-Serbs have come back to Banja Luka but I could say that I had many acquaintances, not all were close friends, but of about 100, 70 have come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Give us a rough guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: A rough number, I know you can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we talking 100, 200, 1.000?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Or 50 or 20?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: You mean the total number who left and have now come back?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: People, your friends, people who you know. My question was how many. You limit it to your friends, and you said 70 per cent. So I would like to know what we are discussing, what number we are discussing, and I would like to know from those, to give me the names who came to you and thanked you for what you have done during the war for those people, for those friends of yours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Well, I've just said, I knew about 100 people and 70 per cent of them have come back to the town. We meet every day. We run into each other in the street, in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Okay. And so the names who came to you? I think you remember at least some of the names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Well, yes. The Osmancevic family, for instance. Eglerovic, Pasalic, I won't go any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Okay. Madam, do you know -- do you know a person -- I don't know if we shouldn't go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On one occasion, I did this on my own free will, but I have to mention names now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: You don't want to mention the names or you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: I do remember. I don't want to mention them in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: M'hm. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: I want to say if we can go into private session, I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: My last question is, I'm sorry, but I must ask this question. I don't want to offend you. Did you ask for this one single case when did you -- when you didn't put the person on the list? Did you ask some extra money for this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Taya has got a few questions for you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: I have only a few questions. All the members in the agency except you were Serb refugees; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992, not only refugees but also resident in Banja Luka, couldn't work because 90 per cent of business didn't function at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: So everybody wanted to find job; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Why all employees except you were Serb refugees? In other words, do you know the reason why other employees than you became to be employed in the agency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: The other employees were refugees because it was on the initiative of refugees that the agency was set up in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milos Bojinovic was also a refugee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Other employees from -- other employees than you, did they make their employment contract with the director, Mr. Milos Bojinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: It wasn't Mr. Bojinovic that we concluded a contract with. He was an employee of the agency like the rest of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Then with whom you and other employees made a contract?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Well, when we registered, when the agency was registered at the court and the municipality, we were automatically registered with the pension fund and the health insurance. That was the system that we had at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: My last question is: Who fixed -- who established the amount of money which should be paid by non-Serbs who are leaving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know. I can't remember exactly, but I think that the director and the man in charge of the financial aspect, but I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And before you leave, I have got a very few questions for you. Your husband, you've told us very little about your husband, madam. You said you didn't know Mr. Brdjanin, you had never met Mr. Brdjanin. Did your husband know Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did your husband have any political connections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How come it was precisely he that was approached by the person you mentioned earlier on and also in your statement and not somebody else, to take part, an active part, in this agency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: They happened to come across each other in town, and this man told him that he was asking the authorities that a bureau be set up for refugees, and that the government had approved this but they said they should organise themselves and find equipment and premises on their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But why you and your husband and not someone else? What expertise, what were your qualifications that put you in better stead or in good stead over others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: We didn't have any special qualifications but the man who ran into my husband on the street knew that we were both out of work because our company had ceased to operate. He knew that we had office space, computers, and telephone lines available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Have you ever heard of Atlas travel agency in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Well, before the war, the Atlas travel agency in Banja Luka were engaged in organising air travel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Putnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they did the same, before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know that both these companies, both these agencies, were closed down before the setting up of your agency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Our agency wasn't at all like those two agencies. Those were agencies that operated before the war. Atlas was, I think it wasn't even a Bosnian agency but a Yugoslav agency, that this was only a representative office or a unit of an agency that was located somewhere else, I don't know where exactly. So these agencies had nothing in common with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that these two agencies were forced to close down before the agency you were responsible for was created, would you accept it? Are you aware that they were forced to close down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: I believe you, but I don't know anything about their being forced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Respective to your offices, where did Atlas and Putnik have their offices? Did they have offices in the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Atlas was in Gospodska Street, because before the war I travelled through Atlas few times and I bought air tickets there. As for Putnik I don't know where that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you in a position to know whether Atlas for example could have provided their offices and equipment to -- for the same purposes that you offered your offices and equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Atlas was not privately owned at the time. Atlas was state-owned. And if they had wanted to provide offices and equipment, they would have had to seek approval from their superiors, but I really don't know, but Atlas and Putnik were state owned agencies, they were not privately owned agencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That must have made it easier for the region or the municipality to take possession of the offices, no? Why not do that once they had been forced to cease operation and offer you to provide premises and equipment? When they could have started -- charity begins at home and would have started by taking over what was theirs in the first place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know, but I think that it would not have been proper for someone's property to be appropriated like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you receive a rent from the government, from the state, for the use of your offices by this agency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No. We had no contacts with the authorities or the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you made available the offices without any co-respective, without any rent, without receiving any rent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ask for some kind of compensation for the use of your offices plus equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No. The only condition was for us to work in the agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the car, did you make the car of the -- your company at the disposal, that you put it at the disposal of the agency as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the only thing that you had in return was the miserable salary that you referred to before? Less than 100 marks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's all? And this is a premises and equipment which, prior to these events, was sufficient for the employ of over 30 persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No, no, no. Not the premises, no, not the premises. Only the equipment, not the premises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you forced in any way that you know and that you could tell us about to make these premises and equipment available to the state? Or was it just something that you voluntarily did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No. It was the local commune that gave us premises, and I put the equipment at the disposal voluntarily, without any force. I saw this as my contribution to help the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Is there a beatification process in your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. favour, by any chance, in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT88
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. I have no further questions, there are no further questions? Okay. I think the witness can leave the courtroom. We need to draw down the curtains before she does. Mr. Ackerman, are there any documents that you need to number or -- no. You finished with yours. Madam I still thank you for having come over to give evidence in this Tribunal and only last thing I have -- I need to tell you is to wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have only very quick thing and it is that we haven't received any decision on our Rule 92 bis motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to refer that to Mr. Ackerman because Mr. Ackerman reserved his position until he was given the list of the witnesses which he was given the last time he was here but we haven't heard from him since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I worked on it as much as I could while I was back in Texas. I think I'll have it finished today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand. All right, okay. Thank you Mr. Ackerman. But we need to know because Donji Vakuf and Prnjavor are soon with us. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Good afternoon, and see you tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
